title: Rivetus and Baron: past-remission persuasio is faith’s fruit, not its justifying instrument
source_text: LXVII. Ex quibus patet Theologos illos, quum fidem definiunt per certam fiduciam, qua unusquisque fidelis firmiter statuit, non solum in genere promissam esse credentibus remissionem peccatorum, sed sibi in particulari concessam; ut facit Andreas Rivetus: aut etiam dicunt talem fiduciam esse verum & proprie dictum fidei salvificae actum; imo esse praecipuum & specificum ejus actum, quae sunt Roberti Baronii verba: mentem tamen eorum non esse persuasionem istam quod peccata nobis remissa sint, esse illum fidei actum quo justificamur: sed illos fidem ita describere, quia talis persuasio est quaedam verae fidei proprietas, quam apta nata est ex se producere, & quae pertinet ad ejus perfectionem. Et quoniam haec persuasio est revera quidam actus fidei justificantis, quo a fide mortua & historica distinguitur, & qui maximi momenti est ad fidelium pacem atque tranquillitatem, & pietatem in eis fovendam; licet justificationem sequatur, non praecedat, nec sit justificationis instrumentum, sed consequens quoddam.
pass_a_gloss: From which it is plain that those theologians, when they define faith by a certain trust by which each believer firmly lays down that remission of sins has been promised not only in general to believers, but granted to himself in particular — as Andreas Rivetus does — or even say that such trust is the true and properly so-called act of saving faith, nay the chief and specific act of it, which are Robert Baron's words: yet their mind is not that that persuasion that sins have been remitted to us is that act of faith by which we are justified; but that they so describe faith because such persuasion is a certain property of true faith, which it is apt by nature to produce from itself, and which pertains to its perfection. And since this persuasion is truly a certain act of justifying faith by which it is distinguished from dead and historical faith, and which is of the greatest moment for the peace and tranquillity of the faithful and for fostering piety in them; although it follows justification, it does not precede it, nor is it the instrument of justification, but a certain consequent.
pass_b_english: Rivetus (and Baron’s stronger wording): faith defined as sure fiducia that remission is granted not only in general but to me in particular — even called saving faith’s chief specific act.
Yet their mind is not that past-tense persuasion (“sins have been remitted”) is the act by which we are justified.
They describe faith that way because such persuasion is a property true faith is apt to produce, and belongs to its perfection.
It is a real act of justifying faith (vs dead/historical), precious for peace and piety — but it follows justification; it is not the instrument.
